title: Numerals, Time, and Dates
summary: The numbers to a thousand and the four things a learner counts with them: the hour, the day of the week, the date, and the year. ¶58 settled which case a numeral governs; here are the numerals themselves.

rules.heading: The Cardinals One to Nine
rules.statement: The first nine numerals are **adjectives in all but name**: they have gender, they decline, and they agree with what they count (¶58). *Vienas* has a singular; the rest are plural in form, since two of a thing are more than one. **Du** is irregular in the feminine — *dvi*, not *dva* — and must be learnt by itself.

paradigms.caption: One to nine, masculine and feminine
paradigms.footnote: *Trys* is the same in both genders, as *šis* is not; it is the only one that does not distinguish them.

examples.target: Turiu du brolius ir dvi seseris.
examples.gloss: I have two brothers and two sisters.
examples.note: the numeral takes the gender of its noun and the case of the sentence

examples.gloss: There are four chairs here.
Two glasses of water are needed.
examples.note: *reikia* puts everything after it in the genitive (¶69), the numeral included

rules.heading: Ten and Upwards
rules.statement: From ten the numerals stop agreeing and start governing: they stand unchanged and put the counted noun in the **genitive plural**, whatever the sentence would otherwise require (¶58). The tens are built on the units, the teens on the units with **-lika**, and *šimtas* and *tūkstantis* are ordinary nouns that happen to mean a hundred and a thousand.

paradigms.caption: Ten to a thousand

cells: vienuolika, dvylika, trylika, keturiolika, penkiolika, šešiolika, septyniolika, aštuoniolika, devyniolika

paradigms.footnote: In a compound number the **last word** decides the construction: *dvidešimt vienas namas* has a singular noun agreeing with *vienas*, while *dvidešimt du namai* has a plural agreeing with *du*, and *dvidešimt penki namai* likewise.

examples.gloss: Fifteen books.
A hundred euros.
Twenty-one people.
examples.note: singular, because *vienas* is the last word

rules.heading: The Ordinals
rules.statement: The **ordinals** — first, second, third — are adjectives outright, declined and agreeing like *geras*. They are what Lithuanian uses for floors, for the hour, and for the day of the month, so they are met far oftener than their English equivalents.

paradigms.caption: The first ten ordinals
paradigms.footnote: Above ten they are formed straightforwardly: *vienuoliktas*, *dvyliktas*, *dvidešimtas*. In a compound only the last word is an ordinal: *dvidešimt pirmas*.

examples.gloss: I live on the first floor.
examples.note: locative, because the floor is a place

examples.gloss: That is the second book.

rules.heading: Telling the Hour
rules.statement: The hour is a **feminine ordinal** agreeing with *valanda*, which is usually left out: *pirma* means one o'clock because *pirma valanda* does. The question is **kelinta valanda?**, literally *the how-manieth hour?* The half hour is *pusė* with the **genitive** of the hour coming, and the minutes before the hour are **be** with the genitive — the Lithuanian counts down to an hour it has not yet reached.

paradigms.caption: Saying the time
paradigms.footnote: *Pusė dešimtos* is half past **nine**, not half past ten. The Lithuanian names the hour being filled, as the clock face does; the English names the one just past. Mistaking this costs an hour.

examples.gloss: What time is it?
I work from eight until five.
We are meeting at two o'clock.

rules.heading: The Accusative of Time
rules.statement: A **point** of time and a **stretch** of time both stand in the accusative, with no preposition. This is the case that answers *kada?* for a single occasion — set it against the plural instrumental of ¶76, which answers the same question for a habit. *Pirmadienį* is on Monday, once; *pirmadieniais* is on Mondays, always.

rows.label: duration
cells: I was in London for a week.

examples.gloss: One day I work, the next I rest.
We lived in Kaunas for a year.

rules.heading: The Days of the Week
rules.statement: The names of the days are built transparently on the ordinals plus **diena**, day — the first day, the second day, and so on from Monday. Only Sunday breaks the pattern. They are masculine, they are written with a small letter, and *pirmadienis* being the **first** day is a reminder that the Lithuanian week begins on Monday.

examples.gloss: On Saturday and Sunday I do not work.
On Fridays we go to a café.

rules.heading: The Months and the Date
rules.statement: The Lithuanian months are **native words**, not the international ones, and most of them name what the country is doing or what the weather is doing — *birželis* is the birch month, *rugpjūtis* the rye-cutting. A date is the **genitive** of the month followed by the ordinal of the day: *sausio penkta*, the fifth of January, literally *January's fifth*.

paradigms.caption: The twelve months
paradigms.footnote: *balandis → balandžio* and *lapkritis → lapkričio* show the softening of *d* and *t* before a back vowel that ¶28 gave for the genitive generally.

examples.gloss: Today is the fifth of March.
We are meeting on the tenth of May.
examples.note: accusative of time on the ordinal

rules.heading: The Year
rules.statement: A year stands in the **instrumental plural** with *metais*, and only the **last** element of the number is made an ordinal. This is the one construction of the level that looks alarming written out, and it is entirely mechanical: read the number as a cardinal until the final word, make that an ordinal, and put both into the instrumental plural.

examples.target: Gimiau tūkstantis devyni šimtai devyniasdešimt penktaisiais metais.
examples.gloss: I was born in 1995.
In the year 2020.

footnotes: In speech the whole phrase is often cut down to the last word: *devyniasdešimt penktaisiais*, in ninety-five.

rules.heading: Prepositions of Time
rules.statement: Three prepositions of time take the **accusative** where those of ¶33 took the genitive. **Prieš** is *ago* or *before*; **per** is *within* a stretch or *during* it. Against them stand the genitive pair **nuo … iki**, from one time to another, which frames a working day or an opening hour.

rows.label: nuo … iki
cells: nuo aštuntos iki penktos — from eight to five

examples.gloss: I came to Lithuania a year ago.
I shall do everything within an hour.
From today until Friday I am not working.

drills.explanation: *du* is masculine; a sister is feminine and takes **dvi**. The numerals one to nine agree in gender with what they count, and *du/dvi* is the pair that must simply be memorised.
The days are ordinals plus *diena*, counting from Monday as the first: *trečiadienis* is the third day. Only *sekmadienis* is outside the pattern.

drills.stem: How is **the fifth of March** written?
drills.explanation: The month goes into the **genitive** and the day is a feminine ordinal: *kovo penkta*, March's fifth. The order is month first, unlike the English.
Half **of the tenth** hour — the hour being filled, not the one just past. It is 9:30. This is the trap of the construction, and it costs an hour every time it is missed.
Numerals from ten up take the genitive **plural**, so *knygų* and not *knygos*. In a compound the last word governs: *vienas* is singular and gives *namas*, so a plural *namai* after it is wrong.

drills.stem: Complete: **Dirbu nuo aštuntos iki ____.** (I work from eight until five.)
drills.explanation: *iki* governs the genitive, and the hour is a feminine ordinal: *penktos*. *penktą* would be the accusative, which is what tells the hour of an appointment (*penktą valandą*), not the end of a range.

drills.stem: **Pirmadienį** and **pirmadieniais** both answer *kada?* What is the difference?
options: *Pirmadienį* is one particular Monday; *pirmadieniais* is Mondays as a rule.
*Pirmadienį* is the past and *pirmadieniais* the future.
drills.explanation: The accusative marks a single occasion (¶83), the plural instrumental a habit (¶76). Lithuanian keeps the two apart by case where English needs the extra words *on* and *on … s*.

drills.stem: Which of these correctly pair a time preposition with its case?
drills.explanation: *po* in the sense *after* takes the **genitive** (¶33); with the instrumental it means *under* (¶75). It never takes an accusative. The rest are right.

drills.stem: **Mes gyvenome Kaune metus.** What does the accusative *metus* express?
options: The point at which they arrived.
The means by which they lived there.
drills.explanation: The accusative of time serves for a **stretch** as well as a point: *metus*, for a year. No preposition answering to English *for* is used or wanted.

drills.stem: In **Gimiau tūkstantis devyni šimtai devyniasdešimt penktaisiais metais**, how many words of the number itself are ordinals?
drills.explanation: One: *penktaisiais*. Everything before it is read as an ordinary cardinal, and only the last element is made an ordinal and put into the instrumental plural along with *metais* (¶86).

drills.title: Antradienio darbotvarkė
drills.passage: Antradienį Rūta dirba nuo aštuntos iki penktos. Ryte ji važiuoja į darbą autobusu — kelionė trunka dvidešimt minučių. Pusę dešimtos ji geria kavą su kolege. Pirmą valandą pietūs. Po pietų ji turi du susitikimus. Šeštadieniais ir sekmadieniais Rūta nedirba; tada ji skaito knygas arba važiuoja pas mamą į Kauną. Gegužės dešimtą jos gimtadienis.
drills.translation: On Tuesday Rūta works from eight until five. In the morning she goes to work by bus — the journey takes twenty minutes. At half past nine she drinks coffee with a colleague. At one o'clock, lunch. After lunch she has two meetings. On Saturdays and Sundays Rūta does not work; then she reads books or goes to her mother's in Kaunas. Her birthday is on the tenth of May.

questions.explanation: *Pusę dešimtos* — half of the tenth hour, that is 9:30. The accusative *pusę* is here because the phrase answers *kada?* for a single occasion (¶83).

questions.stem: Which time expressions in the passage name a **habit** rather than a single occasion?
questions.explanation: The plural instrumentals *šeštadieniais* and *sekmadieniais* mean Saturdays and Sundays in general. *Antradienį* and *gegužės dešimtą* are accusatives naming one particular day.

questions.stem: How many minutes does Rūta's journey to work take?
questions.explanation: *dvidešimt minučių* — twenty. Note the genitive plural *minučių*: from ten upwards a numeral fixes its noun in that case whatever the sentence is doing (¶80), and *t* softens to *č* before the ending.
